```{r}
#| label: footer-options
#| include: false
options(housepi.footer.warranty = TRUE)
options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
```

We start by loading the R package housepi into the session:
```{r}
#| label: import-library
# import the library
library(housepi)
```
The package can be installed following the instruction in the documentation [main page](https://mmmi-pasteur.pages.pasteur.fr/housepi/index.html).

# Format of the data

A dataset should be a data.frame or tibble, with one row per household member.
A minimal dataset looks like this^[
This dataset ships with the "test" model, see `?dummy_household` and `?template_test`.]
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>
```{r}
#| label: dummy-household-data-table
#| echo: false
env <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
utils::data("dummy_household", package = "housepi", envir = env)
knitr::kable(env[["dummy_household"]])
```
</div>
</div>
To group individuals in households, provide a column `"hh_id"` with the respective household tag.
Individuals with the same tag are considered to belong to the same household.
No `"hh_id"` implies that all individuals are treated as if living separately.

A column `"id"` with individual identifiers can be provided to keep track of changes and make errors more readable.
Without it, housepi tags individuals with row numbers.

To perform inference on transmission, a `"status"` must be provided for each individual $i$.
Status $s_{i}$ should be a character, or an integer value satisfying the following convention:
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>
| Status   | $s_{i}$    |
|----------|:- --------:|
| escaped  | `0`        |
| infected | $\geq$ `1` |
| missing  | `NA`       |
</div>
</div>
We can use the status as a label for different classes of infectious household members.
This is used in status-specific latent definitions (see [Data augmentation](data_augmentation.html)).

# A collection of models

To see the list of model templates currently available in housepi, run
```{r}
#| label: list-templates
# present the list of template model name
browse_templates()
```
Each template comes with definitions that can be used straight away or changed.
To know more about each model, choose a name from the previous list and run
```{r}
#| label: model-help
#| eval: false
# open the template help page
browse_templates("final-size")
```
This opens the help page of the template, also reachable with `?template_final_size`.

# The housepi model class

Generate a model object with `new_housepi_model()`:
a dataset can be provided at this point via the `data` argument or attached later with `add_dataset()`.
Here we consider the `flu_1918_frederick` final-size study (a public dataset shipped with housepi, see `?flu_1918_frederick`),
modelled with the [final-size](https://mmmi-pasteur.pages.pasteur.fr/housepi/reference/template_final_size) transmission model:
```{r}
#| label: load-model
# fix the seed to reproduce the results in the current session
set.seed(42)

# set the housepi theme for result visualization
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)

# generate an instance of the final-size model on top of the dataset
hh_model <- new_housepi_model(flu_1918_frederick, "final-size")
```
We can retrieve the template model description by calling `hh_model$help()` at any time.
To move a time-dependent model to discrete time, we pass `discr = TRUE` to `new_housepi_model()` (see [Infectivity profiles](infectivity_profiles.html#discrete-time-models)).

A brief summary of the loaded dataset can be obtained via `summarise_house_cases()`,
here formatted with [flextable](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=flextable):
```{r}
#| label: summarise-house-cases
# show a summary of cases as a `flextable`
summarise_house_cases(hh_model) |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::colformat_double(j = "percent", digits = 1) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ level) |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ level + metric, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(level = "", metric = "", percent = "[%]")) |>
  flextable::autofit()
```
The last row is the count of the equivalence classes,
i.e. households that are indistinguishable by the model^[
Household with the same size, statuses, rates, etc, contribute the same to the likelihood and are thus grouped into equivalence classes.
The likelihood is then evaluated just once per equivalence class, and multiplied by the class size.
A sampled latent variable makes every household a class of its own.].

At any moment we can re-export the full dataset with `get_dataset()`.
```{r}
#| label: import-data
# data associated to the model
head(get_dataset(hh_model))
```

# Associate parameters

Each parameter needs a definition: the prior and the proposal of the MCMC sampler, or a constant value.
We can call `add_parameter()` as follows:
```{r}
#| label: add-parameters
# single parameter definitions
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  # alpha: baseline community transmission rate
  # name: matching the model requirement
  # prior: uniform with default arguments, min = 0, max = 1
  add_parameter(name = "alpha", prior = "uniform") |>
  # beta: baseline person-to-person transmission rate
  add_parameter("beta", prior = "uniform")

# append parameters using multiple definitions
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  # hh_size_ref: reference household size, constant value
  # gamma: size-scaling of person-to-person rate
  add_parameter(hh_size_ref = 6L, gamma = list(prior = "uniform"))

# inspect parameter definitions
hh_model |> get_parameters()
```
A parameter is defined as constant passing its `const` value, e.g. `add_parameter("hh_size_ref", const = 1)`, or as a bare number, as `add_parameter(hh_size_ref = 1)` above.
At any moment we can review the parameter definitions of the model by calling `get_parameters()`.

For further information on the available options for priors and MCMC proposals definitions, see [Priors and proposals](priors_and_proposals.html).

# Run inference

Once the definitions are in place, run the inference with `run_inference()`.
Inference is performed using Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), with the Metropolis-within-Gibbs algorithm [@metropolis_equation_1953; @hastings_monte_1970].
Controls of the MCMC can be provided at this stage, including the number of `steps`, `chains` and `threads`.
The draws come as [posterior](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=posterior) objects that can be accessed to compute estimates.
```{r}
#| label: run-inference
# run the Monte Carlo specifying its settings (equal to default)
hh_fit <- hh_model |>
  run_inference(steps = 2000, # steps per chain, after adaptation
                thin = 10,    # keep one step every ten
                adapt = 1000, # adaptation steps, run before `steps`
                chains = 4,   # independent chains
                threads = 1)  # parallel threads

# set 95% credible intervals (default is 90%, as in `posterior`)
set_housepi_summary(cri_level = 0.95)

# summarise posterior draws of parameters
hh_fit |> summarise_draws()
```

We can extract the parameter draws with `get_parameter_draws()` and plot traces with [bayesplot](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bayesplot):
```{r}
#| label: param-traces
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for alpha and beta parameters across MCMC iterations with four parallel chains overlaid.
# visualize the traces of every chain with 'bayesplot'
get_parameter_draws(hh_fit) |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 1))
```

# Models with data augmentation

Here we present a case study, using the template model "case-ascertained" (see `?template_case_ascertained`) where households are conditioned on a single introduction [@cauchemez_bayesian_2004].
The timing of infections is governed by an [infectivity profile](infectivity_profiles.html).
In this application, the household structure comes from the `sarscov2_2021_icofs` dataset (see `?sarscov2_2021_icofs`).
```{r}
#| label: load-latent-model
# select a data structure (used later for the simulation)
community_structure <- sarscov2_2021_icofs |>
  dplyr::select(id, hh_id)

hh_model <- community_structure |>
  new_housepi_model("case-ascertained") |>
  add_parameter(import = "template") |>
  add_infectivity_profile(import = "template")

# inspect current definitions
hh_model |> get_parameters()
hh_model |> get_infectivity_profiles()
```
Here we passed `import = "template"` to load directly the parameter definitions from the template.

## Model observed and latent quantities

This model is expressed in terms of the infection time `infec_time`, which is typically unobserved and thus require to be modelled as a latent variable.
We do so with Bayesian [data augmentation](data_augmentation.html) [@tanner_calculation_1987] which samples the latent variables alongside parameters.
Latent variables are added with `add_latent()`.
To inform latent variables, we need to add observation models with `add_observation()`, 
e.g. in this case the dates of symptom onset, the study start date corresponding to the first onset.
```{r}
#| label: load-latent-definitions
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  add_latent(
    # infection time, generated by the transmission model,
    # sampled in inference within these bounds
    infec_time = list(min = start_date - 14, max = onset_date + 1),
    # incubation period for each individual
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", mean = 2, sd = 1, max = 14)
  ) |>
  add_observation(
    # observation of onset date noisy around the real onset time
    onset_date = list(discr = TRUE, model = "normal", min = floor(infec_time),
                      mean = infec_time + incub_period),
    # followup starts with earliest onset date (house-level observation)
    start_date = list(func = min(onset_date), level = "house"),
    # followup ends after 3 weeks after first onset
    end_date = start_date + 21
  )
```
Infections are generated by the transmission process, 
so `infec_time` takes no `model`, but only bounds `min` and `max` used by the inference to sample it.
On the contrary, incubation periods are not modelled by the transmission process, so `incub_period` requires a `model`.
The follow-up dates take no `model` either: `func` computes `start_date` from other values, and `level = "house"` gives one value per household, here the earliest onset among its members.

Printing the model lists the definitions in place and the ones still missing:
```{r}
#| label: print-model-state
# print current state of definitions
hh_model
```
By default, if a group rate is not provided, its contribution is assumed homogeneous.
To see how to associate group rates in heterogeneous models, see [Group rates](group_rates.html).
We can overlook these alerts for the rest of the walkthrough.

# Simulate an outbreak

We run a simulation with the method `run_simulation`, using the same community structure from the study.
Each household's outbreak starts from one member drawn at random, its primary case.
The transmission process sets every infection time in simulation, starting from the primary case of each household, infected on day $0$.
Every infected individual gets an incubation period, an infection time and a sampled onset date.
```{r}
#| label: run-simulation
# parameter values of the simulation
true_params <- c(alpha = 1e-3, beta = 0.1, gamma = 1)

# the onset_date observation is sampled automatically
simulated <- hh_model |> run_simulation(true_params)

head(simulated)
```
Parameter values can be passed directly as in the previous example, otherwise they are drawn from the respective priors.

# Inspect the results

We attach the simulated study as a new dataset, so the simulated `onset_date` enters inference as an observation.
```{r}
#| label: inference-simulated
hh_fit <- hh_model |>
  # associate the simulated data to a copy of the model
  add_dataset(simulated) |>
  # run inference using multi-threading
  run_inference(threads = 2)
```
Besides the parameters, the fit holds the per-household joint log-likelihood `log_lik`.

We plot the traces against the values used for the simulation:
```{r}
#| label: validation-traces
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with four chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
library(ggplot2)

# collect original parameters used for the simulation
true_table <- data.frame(parameter = names(true_params), true = true_params)

# extract sample to posterior draws_df
param_draws <- get_parameter_draws(hh_fit)
# use bayesplot to plot the posterior draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(param_draws, facet_args = list(ncol = 1)) +
  geom_hline(data = true_table, aes(yintercept = true))
```

The R-hat diagnostics [@vehtari_rank_normalization_2021] check that the chains converged:
```{r}
#| label: rhat-diagnostics
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  R-hat convergence diagnostics for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with color-coded thresholds.
#|  Color intensity represents R-hat values (≤1.05, ≤1.1, >1.1). Points near 1.0 indicate convergence.
# compute Rhat values associated to inferred parameters
rhat_values <- summarise_draws(param_draws, rhat = posterior::rhat)
# convert to named numeric vector
setNames(rhat_values$rhat, rhat_values$variable) |>
  # use bayesplot to showcase Rhat statistics
  bayesplot::mcmc_rhat() +
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(hjust = 1)
```

Finally, we format the estimates and respective credible intervals with `format_estimates`,
and showcase them next to the true values used for the simulation.
```{r}
#| label: parameter-comparison-table
param_draws |>
  summarise_draws() |>
  # generate a formatted estimate with its credible interval
  format_estimates() |>
  dplyr::select(parameter = variable, inferred = formatted) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(true_table, by = "parameter") |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ parameter, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

Use [posterior predictive checks](predictive_checks.html) to compare observed household measures against measures predicted by the model posterior distribution.

A single inference replica can miss the simulated truth by chance:
validate the inference with [performance checks](performance_checks.html) and [simulation-based calibration](simulation_calibration_checks.html).
